*   **Usage:** Implemented in Unicam (mouse + single button + gestures) and StyleCam (tailored camera positions/paths) [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the 'Cinematic Camera Metaphor' (implied by the context of mouse + button + gestures) was implemented in Unicam (mouse + single button + gestures) and StyleCam (tailored camera positions/paths). Source [S1], specifically section 2.6.1.1, explicitly confirms: 'The Unicam allows users to manipulate the position of the 3D camera using a mouse and only a single button, coupled with different gestures... The StyleCam allows authors to significantly tailor the best possible camera positions and paths...' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
The 3D world moves in correspondence with the 6DoF input device [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that 'The 3D world moves in correspondence with the 6DoF input device'. Source [S1], specifically section 2.6.1.3 'Scene-in-Hand Metaphor', explicitly states: 'With the scene-in-hand metaphor, the three-dimensional world is moved in correspondence with the six degree-of-freedom input device.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
It supports absolute mapping (continuous control) or relative mapping (movement only when a button is depressed) [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the evidence supports the existence of absolute mapping (continuous control) or relative mapping (movement only when a button is depressed). Section 2.6.1.2 of Source [S1] explicitly states: 'They explored both an absolute mapping between the input device and eyeball position, and a relative mapping, in which the viewpoint only changed when a button was depressed.' This directly confirms every fact in the claim.
supported

The Cinematic Camera Metaphor is a navigation technique for non-immersive 3D environments where user input manipulates the position and orientation of a virtual camera to control the user's viewpoint [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the Cinematic Camera Metaphor is a navigation technique for non-immersive 3D environments where user input manipulates the position and orientation of a virtual camera to control the user's viewpoint. Source [S1] explicitly defines the 'Cinematic Camera Metaphor' in section 2.6.1.1 as being used in 'non-immersive 3D environments' where 'mouse movements coupled with modifier keys are generally used to manipulate the position of the virtual camera, which in turn controls the user’s viewpoint of the scene.' The evidence directly supports every part of the claim.
supported
Enhancements include rapid and controlled movement techniques [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that enhancements include 'rapid and controlled movement techniques'. In Source [S1], Section 2.6.1.4 (Flying Vehicle Metaphor), the text explicitly states: 'This technique has been enhanced in various ways, such as allowing for rapid and controlled movement [Mackinlay et al. 1990].' Therefore, the evidence directly supports the claim.
supported
*   If using mouse + keys: Map specific key combinations to tumble (rotation), track (pan), or dolly (zoom) operations [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that if using mouse + keys, specific key combinations can be mapped to tumble, track, or dolly operations. Source [S1], section 2.6.1.1 'Cinematic Camera Metaphor', explicitly states: 'In non-immersive 3D environments... mouse movements coupled with modifier keys are generally used to manipulate the position of the virtual camera... This is generally termed as a cinematic camera metaphor, since the user can tumble, track and dolly a viewpoint'. This directly supports the claim.

This matches the claim exactly.

*   If using 6DoF device: Map device position directly to camera position for Eyeball-in-Hand, or map input to spatial/angular velocity for Flying Vehicle [S1, unofficial].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. Section 2.6.1.2 ('Eyeball-in-Hand Metaphor') states that 'the position of the input device is directly mapped to the position of the virtual camera, or eyeball'. Section 2.6.1.4 ('Flying Vehicle Metaphor') states that 'The input device is used to control the spatial and angular velocity of the vehicle'. Both techniques are discussed in the context of using a six degree-of-freedom (6DoF) input device.
supported

The Eyeball-in-Hand and Scene-in-Hand metaphors were also discussed by Ware and Osborne [S1, unofficial], with the Chameleon device by Fitzmaurice [S1, unofficial] and World-in-Miniature by Stoakley et al. [S1, unofficial] serving as examples.

The evidence explicitly states that Ware and Osborne explored three metaphors, including the 'Eyeball-in-Hand' and 'Scene-in-Hand' metaphors. It further identifies the Chameleon device as an example of eyeball-in-hand navigation (citing Fitzmaurice) and describes the 'World-in-Miniature' as an extension of the scene-in-hand metaphor designed by Stoakley et al. All specific claims in the user's statement are directly corroborated by the text in Source [S1].

An extension, "World-in-Miniature," involves manipulating a hand-held miniature copy of the virtual environment [S1, unofficial].

With this technique, navigation can be accomplished by manipulating a hand-held miniature copy of the virtual environment.' This directly supports every fact in the claim.
